verses.translation: And this one who sits{H3427} upon the throne{H3678} — I saw{H7200} in his right{H3225} hand{H3027} one{H259} scroll{H5612}, sealed{H2856} with seals from within{H6441} and from without{H2351}, with seven{H7651} seals.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The scroll is described as חָתוּם בַּחֲתִימוֹת מִבִּפְנִים וּמִבַּחוּץ — 'sealed with seals from within and from without.' This matches the ancient Israelite double-sealed deed described in Jeremiah 32:10-14, where Jeremiah's deed of purchase (ספר המקנה) had a sealed copy and an open copy. Seven seals parallel the practice of witnesses sealing a legal document. Greek says γεγραμμένον ἔσωθεν καὶ ὄπισθεν κατεσφραγισμένον ('written within and on the back, sealed') — describing WRITING on both sides, not SEALING on both sides. The Hebrew sees a legal deed; the Greek sees a manuscript. No back-translator from Greek would describe sealing on both sides when the Greek describes writing on both sides.

Uses סֵפֶר (sefer, H5612 — 'scroll/document') — the word for a legal document in Jeremiah 32:10-14 (ספר המקנה — 'deed of purchase'). Greek βιβλίον is generic 'book/scroll.' The Hebrew implies a legal deed requiring witnessed seals.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sealed with seals from within and from without' — describes double-sealing. Greek: 'written within and on the back, sealed' — describes writing on both sides with sealing mentioned separately.
Hebrew: 'in his right hand' (ביד ימינו — explicitly 'hand'). Greek: ἐπὶ τὴν δεξιάν ('upon the right') — no explicit 'hand.'
translation_notes: חֲתִימוֹת (chatimot — 'seals') is from the root חתם (chatam, H2856 — 'to seal'). This is a later Hebrew noun form, not the biblical חוֹתָם (chotam, H2368 — 'signet ring/seal'). The form chatimot suggests the act of sealing, not the seal-object itself — the seals as legal attestations, not as physical stamp-rings.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 32:10-14 describes the sealed deed: 'I signed the deed (ספר), sealed it (ואחתם), got witnesses... I took the deed of purchase, both that which was sealed (החתום) and that which was open (הגלוי).' The same vocabulary of sefer + chatam appears here in Revelation 5. The scroll before the throne is a legal deed — a title deed to creation that requires an authorized heir to open.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} messenger{H4397} crying out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963}: Who is worthy to open{H6605} the scroll{H5612} and to break{H7665} its seals?

one_way_hebrew: Uses לִשְׁבֹּר (lishbor — 'to break', H7665) for the seals. Greek has λῦσαι ('to loose/untie'). The Hebrew verb שָׁבַר implies violent, irreversible rupture — breaking a vessel (Jer 19:11), breaking a yoke (Jer 28:2,10), breaking bones (Ex 12:46). A back-translator from Greek λῦσαι ('loose') would use התיר (hitir — 'to untie/release'), NOT the forceful destruction verb שבר. The breaking of seals echoes the breaking of the covenant tablets — an act of sovereign authority.

Uses צֹעֵק (tso'eq — 'crying out', H6817) — the specific Hebrew verb for cries of distress or urgent proclamation (Gen 4:10 — Abel's blood 'cries out'; Ex 2:23 — Israel 'cried out' under slavery; Judg 3:9,15). Greek κηρύσσοντα means 'proclaiming/heralding' — an official announcement. A back-translator from Greek would use מכריז (machriz — 'proclaiming'), not the raw, urgent tso'eq.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἰσχυρόν ('strong/mighty') to describe the messenger — absent in Hebrew. Hebrew just says 'one messenger.'
Hebrew: 'to break' (לשבר) the seals. Greek: 'to loose' (λῦσαι) the seals. Different physical action.
translation_notes: רְאוּיָה (re'uyah — 'worthy') is in the FEMININE form, even though it describes a masculine subject. This is characteristic of Mishnaic Hebrew, where ראויה became an invariable predicate adjective. No back-translator from Greek ἄξιος (masculine 'worthy') would produce this distinctly later Hebrew feminine form. This word appears repeatedly in the chapter (vv. 2, 4, 9, 12) and has no standard Strong's number — it is a post-biblical Hebrew adjective from the root ראה.

verses.translation: And not any one{H259} in the heavens{H8064} or in the earth{H776} was able{H3201} to open{H6605} the scroll{H5612} or to see{H7200} into it.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וְשׁוּם (ve-shum — 'and any/no') — a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew word. Biblical Hebrew would use אִישׁ (ish) or אֶחָד (echad) alone for 'anyone.' The word שום in the sense of 'any' is post-biblical (cf. Mishnah Berachot 1:1 etc.). No back-translator from Greek οὐδείς ('no one') would produce this Mishnaic form.

Uses לִרְאוֹת בּוֹ (lir'ot bo — 'to see INTO it') — the preposition ב implies looking inside, examining the contents. Greek has βλέπειν αὐτό ('to look AT it') — merely seeing the exterior. The Hebrew implies the scroll's contents are what matters; the Greek implies even beholding it is impossible.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in the heavens and in the earth' (two realms). Greek: 'in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth' (ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, οὐδὲ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, οὐδὲ ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς — three realms). Greek adds 'under the earth.'
Hebrew: 'to see into it' (לראות בו). Greek: 'to look at it' (βλέπειν αὐτό). Different prepositions, different meaning.
translation_notes: 'To see into it' preserves the Hebrew preposition ב (be — 'in/into'), which implies examining the contents rather than merely beholding the scroll's exterior.

verses.translation: And I was weeping{H1058} greatly{H3966}, since not one{H259} was found{H4672} who was worthy for this matter{H1697}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֵּיוָן שֶׁ (keiwan she- — 'since/seeing that') — a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew causal conjunction not found anywhere in the biblical Hebrew canon. Biblical Hebrew uses כִּי (ki), יַעַן (ya'an), or עַל אֲשֶׁר (al asher) for 'because/since.' The Greek ὅτι (hoti — 'because') would be rendered as כי by any back-translator. The use of כיון ש is a fingerprint of authentic Hebrew composition in the Second Temple / early rabbinic period.

Uses בוֹכֶה אֲנִי (bocheh ani — 'weeping [am] I') — participle + pronoun word order, placing the emotional state first for emphasis. This is natural Hebrew syntax. Greek ἐγὼ ἔκλαιον ('I was weeping') uses standard Greek word order. The Hebrew emphasis pattern is natural in Hebrew but would not be produced by translation from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'worthy for this matter' (לזה הדבר — vague reference). Greek: 'worthy to open the scroll and to look at it' (ἄξιος ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον οὐδὲ βλέπειν αὐτό — specific reference). The Hebrew uses the general דבר ('matter/thing'); the Greek spells out the specific action.
Greek adds 'nor to look at it' (οὐδὲ βλέπειν αὐτό) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Matter' for davar (H1697) captures the Hebrew's deliberate vagueness — the word encompasses word, thing, matter, affair, legal case. The Hebrew sees this as a legal matter (matching the deed-scroll imagery); the Greek narrows it to a physical action.

verses.translation: And one{H259} of the elders{H2205} said{H559} to me: Do not weep{H1058}! See{H7200}, the lion{H738} which is from the clan{H4940} of Yehudah{H3063}, from the root{H8328} of David{H1732}, has overcome{H5329} to open{H6605} the scroll{H5612} and to break{H7665} the seven{H7651} seals.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת (mi-mishpachat — 'from the CLAN/FAMILY of', H4940). Greek has ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς ('from the TRIBE of'). In the OT social hierarchy, שֵׁבֶט/מַטֶּה (shevet/matteh — 'tribe') is the largest unit, while מִשְׁפָּחָה (mishpachah — 'clan/family') is a subdivision within the tribe (Josh 7:14 — Israel narrows by tribe, then clan, then household). A back-translator from Greek φυλή ('tribe') would use שבט, never the smaller-unit word משפחה. The Hebrew author uses the more precise kinship term — Yehudah's royal CLAN, not the entire tribe.

The manuscript has a lacuna: מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת [  ] יוּדָא — a visible gap between 'clan of' and 'Yehudah.' This physical gap in the Hebrew text is evidence of a manuscript tradition, not a translation — back-translations don't have lacunae.

The spelling יוּדָא (Yuda) rather than the standard יְהוּדָה (Yehudah) is the Aramaic-influenced form found in Ezra 5:1,8 and the Aramaic portions of Daniel. This spelling is characteristic of the Second Temple period and would not be produced by a Greek-to-Hebrew translator, who would use the standard biblical spelling.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the clan' (ממשפחת). Greek: 'from the tribe' (ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς). Different social unit.
Hebrew: 'to break' (לשבר) the seals. Greek: 'to loose' (λῦσαι) the seals — same deviation as verse 2.
translation_notes: 'Clan' for mishpachah preserves the distinction from 'tribe' (shevet). The lion comes from the specific ruling clan within Judah, not from the tribe generically.

'Overcome' for nitsach (H5329) — the root נצח means to prevail, be victorious. The same root appears in the Psalm titles as מְנַצֵּחַ (menatseach — 'choirmaster/director'), connecting victory to worship leadership. The victor is also the worship leader.
textual_notes: Genesis 49:9-10 — 'Judah is a lion's whelp (גּוּר אַרְיֵה יְהוּדָה)... The scepter shall not depart from Judah.' The 'lion from the clan of Yehudah' directly quotes Jacob's blessing. Isaiah 11:1,10 — 'A shoot from the stump of Jesse... the root of Jesse (שֹׁרֶשׁ יִשַׁי) shall stand.' The Hebrew naturally combines these two messianic prophecies.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} in the midst{H8432} of the throne{H3678} and the living-ones{H2416} and the four{H702} and twenty{H6242} elders{H2205}, one{H259} lamb{H7716} standing{H5975} as though slain{H2026}; and to it were seven{H7651} horns{H7161} and seven{H7651} eyes{H5869}, and these are the seven{H7651} spirits{H7307} of YHWH{H3068}, sent out{H7971} into all{H3605} the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses רוּחוֹת יַהְוֶה (ruchot YHWH — 'spirits of YHWH') with the divine name. Greek has τοῦ Θεοῦ πνεύματα ('spirits of God'). A back-translator from Greek θεός ('God') would write אלהים (Elohim), not the tetragrammaton YHWH. The Hebrew connects directly to Zechariah 4:10 — 'These seven are the EYES OF YHWH (עֵינֵי יְהוָה), ranging through the whole earth (מְשׁוֹטְטִים בְּכָל הָאָרֶץ).' The Hebrew author quotes Zechariah's language; the Greek translator replaced YHWH with the generic θεός.

Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716) — the specific Passover lamb word from Exodus 12:3-5 (שֶׂה לְבֵית אָבוֹת — 'a lamb per household'). Greek ἀρνίον is a generic diminutive 'little lamb.' A back-translator would more likely use כֶּבֶשׂ (keves — 'young ram') or טָלֶה (taleh — 'young lamb'). The consistent use of seh throughout this chapter (vv. 6, 8, 12, 13) ties the Lamb directly to the Passover sacrifice.

Uses נֶהֱרַג (neherag — 'slain', niphal of הרג, H2026) — a general verb for killing. Greek ἐσφαγμένον (from σφάζω — 'to slaughter/butcher') specifically means ritual or sacrificial slaughter. Notably, the Hebrew does NOT use שָׁחַט (shachat — 'to slaughter'), which is the specific OT verb for slaughtering the Passover lamb (Ex 12:6). The Hebrew author chose the general 'killed' rather than the sacrificial 'slaughtered' — implying the lamb was murdered, not merely ritually processed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spirits of YHWH' (רוחות יהוה). Greek: 'spirits of God' (τοῦ Θεοῦ πνεύματα). Divine name vs. generic title.

Hebrew: one בְּתוֹךְ (betoch — 'in the midst of') governing throne, living-ones, and elders together. Greek: repeats ἐν μέσῳ ('in the midst') twice — 'in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, AND in the midst of the elders.' Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: 'Living-ones' for chayyot (H2416) — the same word as the living creatures in Ezekiel 1:5-22. The Hebrew author uses the Ezekiel term naturally; the Greek ζῷα ('living beings/animals') is a standard translation.
'Sent out' for nishlach (H7971, niphal) — from the root שלח, the same root as שלוחים (sheluchim — 'sent-ones/apostles' in Rev 21:14). The spirits are 'apostled' into all the earth.
textual_notes: Zechariah 4:10 — 'These seven are the eyes of YHWH, which range through the whole earth.' Also Zechariah 3:9 — 'Upon one stone are seven eyes.' The seven-eyed lamb merges the stone of Zechariah 3 with the eyes of Zechariah 4. Isaiah 11:2 lists the spirit of YHWH in sevenfold description upon the shoot of Jesse — connecting to the 'root of David' in verse 5.

verses.translation: And he came{H935} and took{H3947} the scroll{H5612} from the right{H3225} hand{H3027} of this one who sits{H3427} upon the throne{H3678}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the right hand of this one who sits' (מיד ימינו מזה שיושב). Greek: ἐκ τῆς δεξιᾶς τοῦ καθημένου ('from the right of the one sitting'). Close parallel — one of the few verses where Hebrew and Greek substantially agree.
translation_notes: The Hebrew uses the demonstrative מִזֶּה (mi-zeh — 'from THIS one') emphasizing the immediacy and specificity of the one on the throne. Greek simply says τοῦ καθημένου ('the one sitting').

verses.translation: And in the moment that he took{H3947} the scroll{H5612}, the four{H702} living-ones{H2416} and the four{H702} and twenty{H6242} elders{H2205} were falling{H5307} before{H6440} the lamb{H7716}; and in their hands{H3027} a lyre{H3658} and fire-pans{H4289} full{H4392} of incense{H7004}, and this is the prayer{H8605} of the holy ones{H6918}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — STRONGEST ONE-WAY MARKER IN THE CHAPTER: Uses מַחְתּוֹת (machtot — 'fire-pans/censers', H4289) — the specific Tabernacle/Temple implements for carrying burning coals. These appear in: Lev 10:1 (Nadab and Abihu took their machtah), Lev 16:12 (High Priest on Yom Kippur fills his machtah with coals from the altar), Num 16:6,17-18 (Korah's rebellion — each takes his machtah), Num 16:38-39 (rebel fire-pans hammered into altar covering), 1 Kings 7:50 (Solomon's Temple had golden machtot). Greek has φιάλας χρυσᾶς ('golden BOWLS/vials'). A back-translator from Greek would write קְעָרוֹת זָהָב ('golden bowls'), NOT the Levitical fire-pan term. The Hebrew describes an exact Tabernacle scene: fire-pans filled with incense before the divine presence — this is Yom Kippur in heaven.

Uses כִּינּוֹר (kinnor — 'lyre', H3658) — David's specific instrument (1 Sam 16:16,23; 2 Sam 6:5; Ps 33:2, 43:4, 49:4, 71:22, 81:2, 92:3, 98:5, 108:2, 147:7, 149:3, 150:3). This is the instrument of the Levitical Temple worship orchestrated by David (1 Chr 15:16, 25:1-6). Greek κιθάρας ('harps') is a standard translation but the Hebrew naturally reaches for the Davidic worship instrument. Note Hebrew SINGULAR כינור vs. Greek PLURAL κιθάρας — one lyre shared, not individual harps.

Uses תְּפִילַּת הַקְּדוֹשִׁים ('the PRAYER of the holy ones', H8605) — singular תפילה (tefillah), treating the collective prayers as one unified prayer. Greek has αἱ προσευχαί ('the PRAYERS', plural) τῶν ἁγίων ('of the saints'). A back-translator would use the plural תפילות. The Hebrew singular implies a unified liturgical offering.

Uses וּבְשָׁעָה שֶׁ (u-ve-sha'ah she- — 'and in the moment that') — a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew temporal construction (cf. Mishnah Berachot 1:1). Biblical Hebrew would use כַּאֲשֶׁר (ka'asher — 'when') or בְּ + infinitive. Greek ὅτε ('when') is neutral. No back-translator would produce this Mishnaic idiom.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: מַחְתּוֹת ('fire-pans/censers'). Greek: φιάλας χρυσᾶς ('golden bowls'). Entirely different implements — Levitical fire-pans vs. libation bowls.
Greek adds χρυσᾶς ('golden') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew doesn't specify the material.
Hebrew: singular כינור ('a lyre'). Greek: plural κιθάρας ('harps'). Different number.
Hebrew: singular תפלת ('prayer'). Greek: plural προσευχαί ('prayers'). Different number.
translation_notes: 'Fire-pans' for machtot preserves the Tabernacle connection. These are not bowls for holding liquids but metal implements for carrying burning coals and incense — the same implements used on Yom Kippur when the High Priest enters the Holy of Holies (Lev 16:12-13).
'Lyre' for kinnor — David's instrument, the instrument of Levitical worship. Not a harp (nevel) but a smaller stringed instrument played with a plectrum.
textual_notes: Leviticus 16:12-13 — 'He shall take a fire-pan (מַחְתָּה) full of burning coals from the altar... and two handfuls of finely ground incense (קְטֹרֶת)... He shall put the incense on the fire before YHWH, so that the cloud of incense covers the mercy seat.' Revelation 5:8 describes the identical Yom Kippur scene: fire-pans full of incense before the divine presence.
Psalm 141:2 — 'Let my prayer (תפלתי) be counted as incense (קטרת) before you.' The Hebrew connection between prayer and incense is explicit in both Psalm and Revelation.

verses.translation: And they sang{H2167} a new{H2319} song{H7892} and said{H559}: You are worthy to take{H3947} the scroll{H5612} and to open{H6605} its seals, for you were slain{H2026} and you acquired{H7069} us with your blood{H1818}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שִׁיר חָדָשׁ (shir chadash — 'a new song') — the EXACT phrase from Psalms 33:3, 40:4, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9, 149:1, and Isaiah 42:10. This is one of the most distinctive Psalm phrases in the Hebrew Bible. Greek ᾠδὴν καινήν is a standard translation, but the Hebrew naturally quotes the Psalms. The verb זִמְּרוּ (zimmeru — 'they sang/made music', H2167) is specifically the Psalm-singing verb, used dozens of times in Psalms (Ps 9:12, 18:50, 27:6, 30:5, 47:7, 57:8, 66:2,4, 68:5,33, 98:4-5, 105:2, 108:2, 135:3, 147:1,7, 149:3).

Uses וְקָנִיתָ (ve-qanita — 'and you acquired/purchased', H7069) from קָנָה (qanah). This verb carries a dual meaning in Hebrew: (1) to purchase/acquire (Gen 25:10, 33:19, 47:20), and (2) to create/bring forth (Gen 4:1 — Eve says 'I have acquired/created a man'; Gen 14:19,22 — 'God Most High, creator/acquirer of heaven and earth'; Deut 32:6 — 'Is he not your father who acquired/created you?'; Ps 139:13 — 'You created/acquired my inward parts'). Greek ἠγόρασας ('you bought in the marketplace', from ἀγοράζω) is purely commercial. A back-translator from Greek would use a simpler commercial verb. The Hebrew qanah implies both purchase AND creation — the lamb bought the holy ones and thereby created them anew.

Hebrew: בְּדָמֶיךָ (be-dameicha — 'with your BLOODS', PLURAL). Hebrew דם (dam — 'blood') in its plural form דמים (damim) specifically connotes violently shed blood, bloodguilt, or blood-price (Gen 4:10-11, 2 Sam 3:27-28, Ps 51:16, Isa 1:15). The plural form implies blood shed by violence. Greek ἐν τῷ αἵματί σου uses singular 'blood.' A back-translator would use singular דמך.
greek_deviations: Greek adds τῷ Θεῷ ('to God') after 'you purchased us' — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew says simply 'you acquired us'; the Greek specifies 'you purchased us to God.'

Greek adds ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς καὶ γλώσσης καὶ λαοῦ καὶ ἔθνους ('from every tribe and tongue and people and nation') — the fourfold universal formula is entirely absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew has only 'you acquired US' — intimate and unqualified.
translation_notes: 'Acquired' for qanita rather than 'bought' or 'purchased' — preserving the Hebrew verb's dual creation/purchase semantics. The redeemer both purchases and creates.
'Sang' for zimmeru — the specific Hebrew verb for making music, especially psalm-singing. This is not merely 'saying' or 'chanting' but musical worship.
textual_notes: Psalm 40:4 — 'He put a new song (שיר חדש) in my mouth, a praise to our God.' Psalm 98:1 — 'Sing to YHWH a new song (שיר חדש), for he has done marvelous things; his right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.' The new song in the Psalms is always a response to YHWH's saving acts — matching the context here where the song celebrates the lamb's redemptive act.

verses.translation: And you made{H6213} us priests{H3548} and kings{H4428}, and we shall be kings{H4428} upon the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew order is כֹהֲנִים (kohanim — 'priests') BEFORE מְלָכִים (melachim — 'kings'). Greek order is βασιλεῖς ('kings') BEFORE ἱερεῖς ('priests') — reversed. The Hebrew order matches Exodus 19:6 — מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים ('a kingdom of priests') — where priesthood is the defining role and kingship is the framework. A back-translator from Greek, seeing 'kings and priests,' would preserve that order. The Hebrew author instinctively follows the Torah's priority of priesthood over kingship.

Uses כֹהֲנִים (kohanim, H3548) — the specific OT priestly class descended from Aaron. This is not a generic 'priest' word but the title of the Aaronic/Levitical priesthood with all its duties of sacrifice, intercession, and teaching Torah (Lev 1-7, Deut 33:10, Mal 2:7). The scene in verse 8 (fire-pans, incense, lyres) has already established the priestly setting.
greek_deviations: Hebrew order: priests then kings. Greek order: kings then priests. Reversed priority.
Greek adds τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν ('to our God') — 'you made us kings and priests to our God.' This phrase is absent from Hebrew.
Greek: βασιλεύσομεν ('we shall reign'). Hebrew: נִהְיוּ מְלָכִים ('we shall be kings'). The Hebrew uses a stative (being kings), the Greek uses an active verb (reigning).
translation_notes: 'Priests' before 'kings' follows the Hebrew text's order, which reflects the Torah's theological priority. Israel's identity is priestly before it is royal.
textual_notes: Exodus 19:6 — 'And you shall be to me a kingdom of priests (ממלכת כהנים) and a holy nation.' This foundational covenant declaration shapes the Hebrew author's word order. The redeemed are first and foremost a priesthood.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} and heard{H8085} many{H7235} voices{H6963} from the messengers{H4397} surrounding{H5439} the throne{H3678}, and their number{H4557} was two-thousand{H505} myriads{H7233}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אַלְפַּיִם רְבָבוֹת (alpayim revavot — 'two-thousand myriads' = 20,000,000) — a SPECIFIC number. Greek has μυριάδες μυριάδων καὶ χιλιάδες χιλιάδων ('myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands') — a poetic, indefinite multiplication. A back-translator from Greek's indefinite expression would write רבבות רבבות ואלפי אלפים (revavot revavot ve-alfei alafim), mirroring the Greek pattern. No back-translator would collapse this into the specific number 'two-thousand myriads.'
Uses קוֹלוֹת (qolot — 'voices', PLURAL). Greek has φωνήν (singular 'voice/sound'). Hebrew hears multiple distinct voices; Greek hears one unified sound.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: specific number 'two-thousand myriads' (20 million). Greek: indefinite 'myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands.'
Hebrew: mentions only messengers around the throne. Greek adds 'and the living creatures and the elders' (καὶ τῶν ζῴων καὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων).
Hebrew: 'voices' (plural). Greek: 'voice' (singular).
translation_notes: אַלְפַּיִם (alpayim) is the DUAL form of אֶלֶף (elef — 'thousand'), meaning specifically 'two thousand.' Combined with רבבות (revavot — 'myriads/ten-thousands'), the total is 2,000 × 10,000 = 20,000,000.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:10 — 'A thousand thousands (אֶלֶף אַלְפִין) served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand (רִבּוֹ רִבְבָן) stood before him.' The Hebrew Revelation's specific number may derive from a tradition of calculating Daniel's indefinite numbers into a specific total. Deuteronomy 33:2 — 'YHWH came from Sinai... from the myriads of holiness (מֵרִבְבֹת קֹדֶשׁ).' Myriads of heavenly beings is a Torah concept.

verses.translation: And saying with a great{H1419} voice{H6963}: The lamb{H7716}, the slain one{H2026}, is worthy of strength{H3581} and glory{H3519} and splendor{H8597} and praises{H8416}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew has FOUR attributes: כֹחַ (koach — 'strength'), כָבוֹד (kavod — 'glory'), תִפְאֶרֶת (tiferet — 'splendor'), תְּהִילֹּת (tehillot — 'praises'). Greek has SEVEN: δύναμιν (power), πλοῦτον (riches), σοφίαν (wisdom), ἰσχύν (strength), τιμήν (honor), δόξαν (glory), εὐλογίαν (blessing). The lists share almost no vocabulary overlap. The Hebrew four-fold doxology uses terms from priestly worship; the Greek seven-fold list appears independently composed. No back-translator would reduce seven distinct Greek terms to four different Hebrew terms.

Uses תִפְאֶרֶת (tiferet — 'splendor/beauty', H8597) — the word for the beauty of the priestly garments (Ex 28:2,40 — לְכָבוֹד וּלְתִפְאָרֶת 'for glory and for splendor'). The Hebrew doxology echoes the priestly garment description. Greek has no equivalent in its list — the closest is τιμή ('honor'), which is a different concept.

Uses תְּהִילֹּת (tehillot — 'praises', H8416) — from the root הלל, the same root as the book of Psalms (תְּהִלִּים / Tehillim). Greek has εὐλογίαν ('blessing') — a different concept entirely (praise vs. blessing). A back-translator from εὐλογία would use בְּרָכָה (berachah — 'blessing'), not תהילה.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: four attributes (strength, glory, splendor, praises). Greek: seven attributes (power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, blessing). Substantially different lists with different counts.
Greek adds πλοῦτον ('riches'), σοφίαν ('wisdom'), τιμήν ('honor') — all absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: תפארת ('splendor'). No Greek equivalent. Hebrew: תהילות ('praises'). Greek: εὐλογίαν ('blessing'). Different words.
translation_notes: 'Splendor' for tiferet — the priestly garment word, linking this doxology to the priesthood theme that runs through the chapter.
'Praises' for tehillot — connecting to the Psalms (Tehillim). The lamb receives the praise that the Psalms direct to YHWH.
textual_notes: Exodus 28:2 — 'You shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory (כבוד) and for splendor (תפארת).' The exact pair כבוד + תפארת appears in both the priestly garments and this heavenly doxology, reinforcing the priestly character of the scene.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} the creatures which are in the heavens{H8064} and upon the earth{H776} and beneath{H8478} the earth{H776} and in the sea{H3220} — I heard{H8085} them saying{H559}: To this one who sits{H3427} upon the throne{H3678} and to the lamb{H7716} — glory{H3519} and praises{H8416} and commendation, from everlasting{H5769} to everlasting{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַבְּרִיאוֹת (ha-bri'ot — 'the creatures/creations') — from the root ברא (bara — 'to create'), the Genesis 1:1 creation verb. This is a post-biblical Hebrew noun derived from the most theologically loaded verb in the Torah. Greek κτίσμα ('created thing') is a standard word. A back-translator could use various words; the specific choice of the ברא root ties this doxology to the creation narrative — all that God CREATED now praises the Creator and the Lamb.

CRITICAL: Uses the doxology formula מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting to everlasting') — the signature closing of the Psalm books: Ps 41:14 (closing Book I), Ps 72:19 (Book II), Ps 89:53 (Book III), Ps 106:48 (Book IV). Also 1 Chr 16:36, Neh 9:5. Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages') — a different formula. A back-translator from Greek would write לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים (le-olmei olamim — 'unto ages of ages'), mirroring the Greek genitive construction. No back-translator would produce the Psalm doxology formula me-olam ve-ad olam.

Hebrew has THREE attributes: כָבוֹד (kavod — 'glory'), תְּהִילּוֹת (tehillot — 'praises'), שֶׁבַח (shevach — 'commendation'). Greek has FOUR: εὐλογία (blessing), τιμή (honor), δόξα (glory), κράτος (dominion). Again the lists differ substantially. Hebrew שֶׁבַח (shevach, H7623) is especially common in Aramaic/late Hebrew (Dan 2:23, 4:34,37; Neh 9:5). Greek κράτος ('dominion/might') is an entirely different concept from 'commendation.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three attributes (glory, praises, commendation). Greek: four attributes (blessing, honor, glory, dominion). Different lists, different counts.
Hebrew: me-olam ve-ad olam ('from everlasting to everlasting' — Psalm doxology). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). Different formulae.
Greek adds 'and all things in them' (καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς πάντα) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Creatures' for bri'ot — preserving the creation (ברא) connection. Everything that God spoke into being in Genesis now speaks praise back to him.
'Commendation' for shevach — this word emphasizes verbal praise and laudatory speech, distinguished from tehillah (song-praise) and kavod (weighty glory).
'From everlasting to everlasting' preserves the Psalm doxology formula that Hebrew readers would immediately recognize.
textual_notes: Psalm 106:48 — 'Blessed be YHWH, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting (מן העולם ועד העולם). And let all the people say: Amen!' This final Psalm doxology is echoed here — and the 'Amen' follows immediately in verse 14.

Nehemiah 9:5 — 'Stand up and bless (ברכו) YHWH your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name (שם כבודך), which is exalted above all blessing and praise (ברכה ותהלה).' The same vocabulary cluster (kavod, tehillah, me-olam ve-ad olam) appears in both texts.

verses.translation: And the four{H702} living-ones{H2416} answered{H6030}: Amen{H543}. And the four{H702} and twenty{H6242} elders{H2205} fell down{H5307} and prayed{H6419} to this one who lives{H2416} from everlasting{H5769} to everlasting{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עוֹנִים (onim — 'answering/responding', H6030) — the specific Hebrew liturgical verb for responsive worship. In Deuteronomy 27:14-26, the Levites speak and all Israel 'answers' (ענה) 'Amen.' In 1 Chronicles 16:36, 'all the people said Amen and praised (הלל) YHWH.' In Nehemiah 5:13, 8:6, the people 'answered' Amen. Greek ἔλεγον means simply 'were saying.' A back-translator from Greek would use אומרים (omerim — 'saying'), NOT the liturgically loaded ענה ('to answer'). The Hebrew implies a responsive liturgy — the living-ones ANSWER the universal doxology of verse 13 with the liturgical Amen.

Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying', H6419, hitpael of פלל) — the specific Hebrew verb for intercessory/liturgical prayer (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10,26-27, 1 Kings 8:28-30, Dan 9:4,20). Greek has προσεκύνησαν ('they worshipped/bowed down'). Prostration and prayer are different actions. A back-translator from Greek would use השתחווה (hishtachaveh — 'bowed down/worshipped'), NOT the prayer verb התפלל. The Hebrew sees the elders engaged in PRAYER — active intercession — not mere prostration.

Again uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting to everlasting') — the Psalm doxology formula, now describing the eternal life of the one on the throne. This formula was used for the doxology in verse 13; now it describes the one who receives it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'answering' (עונים — responsive liturgy). Greek: 'were saying' (ἔλεγον). Different verbs with different liturgical implications.
Hebrew: 'praying' (מתפללים — active prayer). Greek: 'worshipped' (προσεκύνησαν — prostration). Different actions.

Hebrew: 'to this one who lives from everlasting to everlasting' (לזה שחי מעולם ועד עולם). Greek: 'the one living unto the ages of the ages' (ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων). Different formulae, and Greek omits the 'from' — only saying 'into' the ages.
translation_notes: 'Answered' for onim — preserving the responsive liturgical sense. The living-ones do not merely speak; they respond to the creation-wide praise with the covenantal affirmation 'Amen.'

'Prayed' for mitpallelim — the hitpael of פלל carries a reflexive/intensive sense, implying earnest, whole-being prayer. This is the same verb Hannah uses (1 Sam 1:10), Solomon uses at the Temple dedication (1 Kings 8:28), and Daniel uses in exile (Dan 9:4).
textual_notes: 1 Chronicles 16:36 — 'Blessed be YHWH the God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting (מן העולם ועד העולם). And all the people said Amen (ויאמרו כל העם אמן) and praised YHWH (והלל ליהוה).' This scene — the Psalm doxology formula followed by the congregational Amen — is the precise liturgical pattern reproduced in Revelation 5:13-14.

Nehemiah 8:6 — 'And Ezra blessed YHWH the great God, and all the people answered (ויענו) Amen, Amen, lifting their hands; and they bowed their heads and worshipped (וישתחוו) YHWH with their faces to the ground.' The Hebrew Revelation's sequence (answering Amen + falling down + praying) follows this Nehemiah worship pattern.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 5 in Hebrew is saturated with Temple/Tabernacle liturgical vocabulary and Psalm doxology patterns that could not plausibly derive from back-translation of the Greek text. The strongest one-way markers are: (1) מַחְתּוֹת (machtot — 'fire-pans/censers', v8) vs. Greek φιάλας ('bowls') — the Levitical Yom Kippur implement has no connection to the Greek word; (2) מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת ('from the clan', v5) vs. Greek φυλῆς ('tribe') — a more specific kinship term no back-translator would choose; (3) רוּחוֹת יַהְוֶה ('spirits of YHWH', v6) quoting Zechariah 4:10, where Greek substitutes the generic θεός; (4) the Psalm doxology formula מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם (vv. 13-14) vs. Greek εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων; (5) כֹהֲנִים before מְלָכִים ('priests before kings', v10), following Exodus 19:6 priority against the Greek order; (6) the sealed-deed language of verse 1 echoing Jeremiah 32:10-14; (7) לִשְׁבֹּר ('to break', vv. 2,5) vs. Greek λῦσαι ('to loose') for the seals; (8) קָנִיתָ ('you acquired/created', v9) vs. commercial Greek ἠγόρασας ('you bought'). The chapter also contains multiple distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew forms — רְאוּיָה (worthy, feminine invariable), כֵּיוָן שֶׁ (since), בְשָׁעָה שֶׁ (in the moment that), שׁוּם (any) — that fingerprint authentic Hebrew composition in the Second Temple period, not back-translation. The attribute lists consistently differ between Hebrew and Greek (4 vs. 7 in v12; 3 vs. 4 in v13), ruling out translation in either direction. The Hebrew text presents a coherent Yom Kippur-in-heaven scene: the Passover lamb (שה) stands before the throne as High Priest, the fire-pans (מחתות) carry incense (קטורת) = prayer (תפלה), the lyre (כנור) of David accompanies the new song (שיר חדש) of the Psalms, and the elders answer Amen (עונים אמן) in the pattern of 1 Chronicles 16:36 and Nehemiah 8:6.
